claim: `git init` creates an empty repository: a `.git` directory with subdirectories for objects, refs/heads and refs/tags, plus an initial branch that has no commits in it yet.

reasoning: git-init(1) OPTIONS: '--bare  Create a bare repository.' git-clone(1) --bare confirms a bare repository has nowhere to check out a working tree.

claim: Re-running `git init` inside an existing repository is safe and does not overwrite what is already there.
reasoning: git-init(1): 'Running git init in an existing repository is safe. It will not overwrite things that are already there.'

claim: `git clone` creates a new directory, copies the source repository's history, creates remote-tracking branches for the source's branches, sets `remote.origin.url`, and checks out a starting branch.
reasoning: git-clone(1) DESCRIPTION: 'Clones a repository into a newly created directory, creates remote-tracking branches for each branch in the cloned repository ... and creates and checks out an initial branch'; and 'This default configuration is achieved by creating references to the remote branch heads under refs/remotes/origin and by initializing remote.origin.url and remote.origin.fetch'.

claim: `git clone` key options `--branch <name>`, `--depth <n>`, `--single-branch`, `--bare` exist and mean what the table says.
reasoning: git-clone(1): '-b <name>, --branch <name>' points HEAD at that branch (checked out in a non-bare repo); '--depth <depth> Create a shallow clone with a history truncated to the specified number of commits'; '--[no-]single-branch' in SYNOPSIS; '--bare Make a bare Git repository'.

claim: `git status` option `-b` means 'show branch'.
reasoning: git-status(1): '-b, --branch  Show the branch and tracking info even in short-format.' The long format already prints the branch, so '-b show branch' misstates what the flag adds. Prose corrected to 'show branch and tracking info even in short format'.

claim: `git status` `-s` gives short format.
reasoning: git-status(1): '-s, --short  Give the output in the short-format.'

claim: `git status` reports the three states under the headings 'Changes to be committed', 'Changes not staged for commit' and 'Untracked files'.
reasoning: Pro Git 2.2 shows all three headings in real git status output and names them in the surrounding prose ('under the “Changes to be committed” heading', 'a section named “Changes not staged for commit”', 'under the “Untracked files” heading').

claim: `git add` `-A` stages all changes including deletions; `-u` restricts to paths already tracked; `-p` chooses hunk by hunk.
reasoning: git-add(1): '-A, --all ... This adds, modifies, and removes index entries to match the working tree'; '-u, --update  Update the index just where it already has an entry ... but adds no new files'; '-p, --patch  Interactively choose hunks of patch between the index and the work tree'.

claim: `git add` copies a file's content as it is at that instant, so edits made after `add` are not in the commit until the file is added again.
reasoning: Pro Git 2.2: 'If you commit at this point, the version of the file at the time you ran git add is what will be in the subsequent historical snapshot', and the worked example shows the same file listed under both 'Changes to be committed' and 'Changes not staged for commit' after a post-add edit.

claim: `git commit -a` auto-stages modifications and deletions of already-tracked files and never adds a new untracked file.
reasoning: git-commit(1): '-a, --all  Automatically stage files that have been modified and deleted, but new files you have not told Git about are not affected.'

claim: `git add` on a path matched by `.gitignore` is refused rather than silently honoured when the path is named explicitly.
reasoning: git-add(1): 'The git add command will not add ignored files by default. If any ignored files were explicitly specified on the command line, git add will fail with a list of ignored files. Ignored files reached by directory recursion or filename globbing ... will be silently ignored', with '-f, --force  Allow adding otherwise ignored files.'

claim: Repeating `-m` on `git commit` produces extra paragraphs, and `-m` is mutually exclusive with `-c`, `-C` and `-F`.
reasoning: git-commit(1): '-m <msg>, --message=<msg> ... If multiple -m options are given, their values are concatenated as separate paragraphs. The -m option is mutually exclusive with -c, -C, and -F.'

reasoning: git-log(1): 'output is given in reverse chronological order by default'; '<revision-range> ... When no <revision-range> is specified, it defaults to HEAD (i.e. the whole history leading to the current commit).'

claim: A commit carries a link to its parent commit, 'two parents, for a merge commit'.
reasoning: git-merge(1) NAME: 'Join two or more development histories together' — an octopus merge commit has three or more parents, so 'two parents, for a merge commit' states a universal that is not universal. reasoning: Git 2.23.0 release notes: 'Two new commands "git switch" and "git restore" are introduced to split "checking out a branch to work on advancing its history" and "checking out paths out of the index and/or a tree-ish" ... out of the single "git checkout" command.'

claim: `git branch` options `-a` local plus remote-tracking, `-r` remote-tracking only, `-d` delete if merged, `-D` delete regardless, `-m` rename.
reasoning: git-branch(1): '-a, --all  List both remote-tracking branches and local branches'; '-r, --remotes'; '-d, --delete  Delete a branch. The branch must be fully merged'; '-D  Shortcut for --delete --force'; '-m, --move  Move/rename a branch'.

claim: `git switch` aborts rather than silently losing local modifications.
reasoning: git-switch(1): 'Switching branches does not require a clean index and working tree ... The operation is aborted however if the operation leads to loss of local changes, unless told otherwise with --discard-changes or --merge.'

claim: `git branch -d` refuses a branch 'whose commits are not merged'; `-D` deletes it anyway 'and the commits become unreachable from any branch'.
reasoning: Two defects. (a) git-branch(1) states the actual criterion: 'The branch must be fully merged in its upstream branch, or in HEAD if no upstream was set' — not 'merged' in the abstract, so -d can refuse a branch whose commits are reachable from a third branch. (b) In that case the commits stay reachable after -D, so 'become unreachable from any branch' is false as a universal; and unreachable commits remain recoverable via the reflog until they are pruned. Prose corrected to the upstream/HEAD criterion, 'commits that were reachable only from that branch', and reflog recovery.

claim: A branch is a movable pointer stored as a file of a few dozen bytes under `refs/heads/`.
reasoning: Pro Git 3.1: 'A branch in Git is simply a lightweight movable pointer to one of these commits ... a simple file that contains the 40 character SHA-1 checksum of the commit it points to ... as quick and simple as writing 41 bytes to a file.'

reasoning: git-merge(1): 'With --ff, when possible resolve the merge as a fast-forward (only update the branch pointer to match the merged branch; do not create a merge commit). When not possible ... create a merge commit.' --ff is the default.

claim: `--no-ff` always creates a merge commit, `--ff-only` refuses unless the merge fast-forwards, `--abort` backs out of a conflicted merge.
reasoning: git-merge(1): 'With --no-ff, create a merge commit in all cases'; 'With --ff-only, resolve the merge as a fast-forward when possible.
